Tesco's position in the UK grocery market shows how scale can be both a strength and a constraint. Its buying power lets it negotiate lower supplier prices, which supports the Aldi Price Match scheme it introduced to defend market share. At the same time, that scale makes the business slower to respond than discount rivals, whose narrow ranges keep operating costs low.

Applying Porter's Five Forces, buyer power is high because switching costs between supermarkets are close to zero. The threat of substitutes is moderate: online delivery services and convenience stores compete for the same weekly spend. Supplier power is low for most categories, although this changed briefly during the 2022 inflation spike when some branded manufacturers pushed back on price cuts.

Overall, the analysis suggests Tesco's main strategic risk is not new entrants but the gradual erosion of its mid-market customers toward discounters.

During our group project I took on the role of coordinator, mostly because nobody else volunteered in the first meeting. Looking back, this was useful but also uncomfortable. I had to chase people for their sections and I worried that I was coming across as bossy.

Using Tuckman's model, our team clearly went through a storming stage in week three, when two members disagreed about whether to focus the report on sustainability or on cost. I suggested we split the analysis so both views were included, which calmed things down but probably made the final report less focused.

If I did the project again I would agree on clear roles and deadlines in the very first session. I also learned that conflict is not always negative; the disagreement forced us to justify our recommendations with better evidence.

A PESTLE analysis of the electric vehicle market in Australia highlights several factors that will shape demand over the next five years. Politically, the National Electric Vehicle Strategy and the new vehicle efficiency standard create pressure on manufacturers to supply more low-emission models. Economically, high interest rates have reduced household borrowing capacity, which slows uptake of vehicles that still carry a price premium.

Social attitudes are shifting, particularly among younger urban buyers, but range anxiety remains a real barrier in regional areas. Technologically, battery costs continue to fall, although charging infrastructure outside capital cities is patchy. Legal and environmental factors are closely linked: stricter emissions reporting obligations for large companies may encourage fleet operators to electrify earlier than private consumers.

Taken together, these factors point to steady rather than rapid growth, concentrated in metropolitan fleet and premium segments.

Stakeholder mapping is a practical tool for deciding where management attention should go. In the case of the proposed warehouse automation project, employees on the picking floor have high interest but relatively low formal power, whereas the board and the main logistics customer have both high power and high interest.

Mendelow's matrix suggests the company should manage the board and key customer closely, keep the union informed and satisfied, and invest in regular communication with warehouse staff. The risk of ignoring the staff group is that resistance appears late, through absenteeism or informal slowdowns, which can undermine the expected productivity gains.

A realistic recommendation is to involve team leaders in the pilot design. This gives employees a voice, surfaces practical problems early, and builds credibility for the wider roll-out.

Netflix's shift to an advertising-supported tier is a good example of a company changing its revenue model in response to market saturation. For years the business relied almost entirely on subscription growth, but by 2022 subscriber numbers in mature markets had flattened and competition from Disney+, Amazon and local streamers had increased.

The ad tier allows Netflix to reach more price-sensitive customers while creating a second income stream. However, it also introduces new risks. Advertising revenue is cyclical and depends on the wider economy, and the company has limited experience selling ads compared with established media groups.

From a strategic perspective, the move can be seen as a product development strategy within Ansoff's matrix: offering a modified product to an existing market. Its success will depend on whether the extra advertising income outweighs any downgrading by current full-price subscribers.

The marketing mix for a new plant-based snack brand needs to balance premium positioning with mass-market reach. On product, the key differentiator should be taste rather than health claims, since research shows many consumers are sceptical of products that feel like a compromise.

Price should sit slightly above mainstream crisps but below specialist health food brands, signalling quality without excluding regular supermarket shoppers. For place, an initial launch through convenience stores near universities and gyms would target the most likely early adopters before seeking national supermarket listings.

Promotion should rely heavily on sampling and short-form social video, as the brand has a limited budget. Influencer partnerships could help, but they should be chosen for credibility with the target audience rather than follower count alone.

When I started this course I assumed leadership mainly meant being confident and making decisions quickly. The readings on transformational and servant leadership have changed how I think about it. In my part-time job at a café, the manager I respect most rarely gives orders; instead she explains why a task matters and asks for our ideas.

This fits Greenleaf's idea that leaders should prioritise the growth of their team. However, I also noticed that on very busy shifts a more directive approach works better, which supports situational leadership theory. Nobody wants a discussion about values when there are twenty coffees waiting.

My main takeaway is that effective leadership is flexible. I want to practise adjusting my style to the situation rather than assuming one approach suits every team or context.

Financial ratio analysis of the company over the last three years shows a business that is profitable but increasingly stretched. The gross margin has remained stable at around 38 per cent, suggesting pricing power has held up despite rising input costs. However, the current ratio has fallen from 1.6 to 1.1, which indicates weaker short-term liquidity.

The main driver appears to be a build-up of inventory, with inventory days increasing from 54 to 81. This may reflect deliberate stockpiling to avoid supply chain disruption, but it also ties up cash that could be used elsewhere. Gearing has also risen after the company financed a new distribution centre with long-term debt.

Investors should therefore treat the strong profit figures with some caution. Unless working capital management improves, the business could face cash flow pressure if sales slow.

Corporate social responsibility is often presented as a win-win, but the evidence is more mixed. Carroll's pyramid suggests firms have economic, legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities, yet in practice these can conflict. A fashion retailer that commits to paying living wages across its supply chain may face higher costs that competitors avoid.

Some studies find a positive link between CSR and long-term financial performance, often explained through reputation and employee loyalty. Others argue the relationship is weak once firm size and industry are controlled for. There is also the problem of greenwashing, where companies publicise small initiatives while their core operations remain unchanged.

A balanced conclusion is that CSR can create value when it is connected to the firm's core business and backed by transparent reporting, rather than treated as a marketing exercise.

Hofstede's cultural dimensions help explain some of the difficulties our case company faced when it expanded from Germany into Japan. Germany scores relatively low on power distance and high on individualism, whereas Japan scores higher on uncertainty avoidance and places more weight on group harmony.

German managers used direct feedback in meetings, which Japanese staff experienced as confrontational. Decisions also took longer than head office expected, because Japanese colleagues sought broad agreement before committing. Rather than seeing this as inefficiency, the company eventually recognised that the consensus process reduced implementation problems later.

Although Hofstede's framework has been criticised for oversimplifying national cultures, it gave the managers a useful starting point. The more important lesson was the need for local leadership and cross-cultural training before entering the market.

The decision to outsource customer service to an offshore provider should be judged on more than direct labour savings. The business case presented by the operations team estimates a 35 per cent reduction in call centre costs, but it does not include transition costs, quality monitoring or the potential effect on customer satisfaction.

Transaction cost economics suggests outsourcing makes sense when tasks are standardised and easy to monitor. Simple enquiries such as order tracking fit this description. Complex complaints, however, require product knowledge and discretion, and handing these to a third party may increase escalations and churn.

A hybrid model may therefore be more appropriate: outsource routine contacts while keeping complex and high-value customers in-house. The company should also set clear service level agreements and review performance after the first six months.

Change management theory offers useful guidance for the hospital's move to a new electronic records system. Kotter's eight-step model emphasises creating urgency, building a guiding coalition and generating short-term wins. In this case, urgency already exists because the old system is no longer supported by the vendor.

The biggest risk is clinician resistance. Doctors and nurses are already under time pressure, and any system that adds clicks to their workflow will be resented. Involving respected clinicians as champions, and running the pilot in a ward that is open to change, could produce early success stories that persuade others.

Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze model is also relevant, as the hospital must reinforce new routines after go-live. Without ongoing training and support, staff may develop workarounds that undermine the benefits of the system.

Looking at the start-up pitch from a venture capital perspective, the strongest part of the proposal is the founding team's industry experience. Both founders have worked in agricultural logistics, which gives them credibility with farmers and an understanding of the operational problems the platform aims to solve.

The weakest element is the revenue model. The plan assumes farmers will pay a monthly subscription, but many small producers operate on thin margins and may resist another fixed cost. A transaction fee charged to buyers could reduce this barrier.

The market sizing also looks optimistic, as it treats the whole regional agricultural sector as addressable rather than the segment likely to adopt digital tools in the next few years. With a more conservative forecast and a clearer path to break-even, the proposal would be considerably more convincing.

Supply chain resilience became a board-level issue after the pandemic exposed how dependent many firms were on single suppliers. The traditional focus on lean, just-in-time inventory reduced costs but left little buffer when disruption occurred.

In response, companies have explored strategies such as dual sourcing, near-shoring and holding strategic safety stock. Each involves trade-offs. Dual sourcing increases resilience but can weaken purchasing leverage, while near-shoring may raise unit costs even as it shortens lead times.

For the manufacturer in this case study, the most sensible approach is to segment components by risk. Critical parts with long lead times justify extra inventory and a second supplier, whereas low-value commodity items can remain on a lean model. This targeted approach improves resilience without abandoning the efficiency gains of the past two decades.

I found the negotiation simulation one of the most useful activities this semester. Before it, I thought of negotiation as trying to win as much as possible. In the exercise my partner and I focused only on price at first and quickly reached a deadlock.

Things improved when we started asking about each other's interests, as Fisher and Ury recommend. It turned out the other side cared more about delivery timing than price, so we could offer faster delivery in exchange for a better rate. This was a clear example of moving from positional bargaining to an interest-based approach.

I also realised that I tend to make concessions too early when there is silence. Next time I want to prepare my walk-away point in advance and be more comfortable pausing before responding.

Pricing strategy for a subscription software product involves balancing customer acquisition with long-term revenue. A freemium model can attract a large user base quickly, but conversion rates to paid plans are often below five per cent, which means the free tier must be cheap to support.

Value-based pricing, where tiers are linked to the outcomes customers achieve, tends to work better for business clients than simple per-user pricing. For example, a project management tool might price according to the number of active projects rather than seats, which better reflects the value delivered.

The company should also consider price anchoring by introducing a premium enterprise tier. Even if few customers choose it, its presence can make the mid-tier plan appear better value. Regular testing of price points will be needed, as customers' willingness to pay changes as the market matures.
